source_title: The impact of teach-back on comprehension of discharge instructions and satisfaction among emergency patients with limited health literacy: A randomized, controlled study
source_setting: Adult ED patients with limited health literacy at Barnes-Jewish Hospital, St. Louis
source_period: Study period not stated in abstract
source_n: Adult patients with limited health literacy; exact randomized n not exposed in inspected abstract
quantity: Teach-back effect on comprehension of post-ED medication instructions
source_evidence_basis: Abstract reports ordinal regression; medication-comprehension difference statistically significant.
limitations: Abstract-only result; effect size and arm denominators unavailable in inspected abstract; single ED population.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent medication comprehension as a discharge communication checkpoint; do not infer individual probability or effect magnitude.

source_title: Increased Access to Professional Interpreters in the Hospital Improves Informed Consent for Patients with Limited English Proficiency
locator: Abstract, Key Results; Methods, Study Population
source_setting: Inpatients undergoing invasive cardiovascular, general surgery or orthopedic procedures at academic hospital; Chinese- and Spanish-speaking LEP patients
source_n: 152 LEP patients (84 pre, 68 post); post-implementation English comparison n=86
quantity: Adequate informed consent after bedside interpreter-phone implementation
value: 54% post vs 29% pre; p=0.001; adjusted OR 2.56 (95% CI 1.15-5.72)
source_evidence_basis: Adequacy required all three patient-reported elements: understanding reasons, risks, and all questions answered.
limitations: Prospective nonrandomized pre-post study; self-reported consent and propensity adjustment cannot eliminate confounding; intervention improved but did not erase disparity (post LEP vs English aOR 0.38).
inferred_scenario_use: For procedures, include access to a qualified interpreter and understanding of rationale/risks/questions in consent pathway; do not treat language group as a persona or prediction.

source_title: Adequacy of Hospital Discharge Summaries in Documenting Tests with Pending Results and Outpatient Follow-up Providers
locator: Abstract, Main Results; Methods, pending test sample
source_setting: General medicine discharges from two large academic centers in Indianapolis, Indiana
source_n: 696 sampled; 668 analyzed; discharge summaries available for 99.2% of 668; 2,927 pending tests
quantity: Pending tests mentioned in discharge summaries
value: 482/2,927 = 16%; summaries mentioned any pending test in 25%; all tests in 13%
unit: tests and percent; discharge summaries and percent
source_evidence_basis: The original PubMed abstract returned by NCBI EFetch states 482/2,927 tests (16%) were mentioned; 25% of summaries mentioned any pending tests, 13% all; follow-up provider information was documented in 67% of summaries.
limitations: Retrospective random sample at two academic centers; study period and exact summary denominator are not in the inspected abstract. Documentation does not prove completed follow-up or patient notification.
inferred_scenario_use: Close discharge by naming pending test, responsible follow-up clinician, expected timing, and escalation/contact plan.

source_title: Impact of Automated Alerts on Follow-Up of Post-Discharge Microbiology Results: A Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial
locator: Abstract, Key Results; Methods, design and measures
source_setting: 777-bed academic hospital, Boston; positive under/untreated microbiology results after discharge
source_n: 157 results from patients of 121 physicians (intervention 97; control 60)
quantity: Documented follow-up within 3 days of post-discharge microbiology result
value: 27/97 (28%) intervention vs 8/60 (13%) control; adjusted OR 3.2 (95% CI 1.3-8.4), p=0.01
source_evidence_basis: Cluster randomized alert trial; outcome documentation within 3 days.
limitations: Single site; physician ID odd/even pseudo-random allocation; follow-up remained low; documented care only. DOI intentionally omitted pending verification.
inferred_scenario_use: A callback/result workflow should assign a named owner, alert, acknowledgment, patient/provider communication, action, and escalation; alerts alone do not close every loop.

source_title: Does health information technology improve acknowledgement of radiology results for discharged Emergency Department patients? A before and after study
source_period: One month before and one month after eRA implementation; dates not stated in inspected abstract
quantity: Documented acknowledgement of radiology reports for discharged ED patients
source_evidence_basis: Original full text XML reports pre period 70.6% (1,167/1,654), post period 100% (1,423/1,423), and calls the increase 30.4 percentage points (95% CI 28.1–32.6). The reported pre/post percentages imply 29.4 percentage points, so the source delta conflicts arithmetically; retain both statements and block quantitative calibration.
limitations: Uncontrolled before-after study. The published 30.4 percentage-point increase conflicts with its rounded rates (100.0−70.6=29.4); acknowledgment measures receipt, not interpretation, appropriate action, or patient notification.
inferred_scenario_use: Track receipt acknowledgment separately from interpretation, action, and patient contact; exclude reported change magnitude from calibration until source discrepancy is resolved.

source_title: The impact of teach-back on patient recall and understanding of discharge information in the emergency department: the Emergency Teach-Back (EM-TeBa) study
source_setting: Urban non-academic ED; adults discharged with new medical problem
quantity: Patients leaving ED with at least one comprehension deficit
source_evidence_basis: Original full text XML abstract reports 483 participants (239 control, 244 teach-back) and says the proportion leaving with at least one comprehension deficit declined from 49% to 11.9% after teach-back.
limitations: Single-center nonrandomized pre-post comparison, unblinded; language-barrier patients excluded, limiting applicability to interpreter-mediated communication. Does not establish distal outcomes.
inferred_scenario_use: Use teach-back to identify/correct comprehension gaps before discharge; excluded language-barrier patients mean this does not establish effectiveness when interpreters are used.

source_title: Quick Safety 52: Advancing Safety with Closed-loop Communication of Test Results
source_setting: Official Joint Commission safety guidance for accredited organizations
quantity: Recommended closed-loop test result communication components
value: Named responsible clinician; verbal notification and positive receipt for life-threatening findings; timed escalation/back-up; patient-facing contextual explanation and support
source_evidence_basis: Joint Commission Quick Safety recommends backup handoffs, consistent assigned follow-up, confirmation of receipt, timed escalation and avoiding portal-only notification.
limitations: Informational guidance, not a standard or controlled evaluation; recommendations need local workflow and clinical urgency definitions.
inferred_scenario_use: Define status transitions: pending -> received -> acknowledged -> interpreted -> patient/provider informed -> action complete; escalate unacknowledged results.
